# 4.9 Performance Evaluation

The Sharpe ratio, the Treynor ratio, Jensen's alpha and the information ratio; which measure to use when; benchmarks and factor exposures; luck and skill; survivorship bias.

Key file: https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/ai/en/lessons/4.9-key.md

## Risk-adjusted returns

One fund returned 15% last year and another 10%. Is the first one necessarily better? Not necessarily: the first may have taken far more risk. Evaluating performance means looking at risk-adjusted returns. Let the fund's average return be $\bar R_p$ and the risk-free rate $r_f$:

- The Sharpe ratio (Sharpe ratio, Sharpe, 1966): $S_p = \frac{\bar R_p - r_f}{\sigma_p}$, the excess return per unit of total risk.
- The **Treynor ratio** (Treynor, 1965): $T_p = \frac{\bar R_p - r_f}{\beta_p}$, the excess return per unit of systematic risk.
- **Jensen's alpha** (Jensen, 1968): $\alpha_p = \bar R_p - [r_f + \beta_p(\bar R_M - r_f)]$, the part of the actual return above the security market line (alpha), usually estimated by the intercept of a regression.
- The **information ratio**: $IR_p = \frac{\alpha_p}{\sigma(e_p)}$, alpha divided by the standard deviation of the residual, that is, the alpha earned per unit of firm-specific risk. It is also often computed as the average return over a benchmark divided by the **tracking error** (the standard deviation of the difference from the benchmark's return).

To make the Sharpe ratio easier to read, Modigliani and Modigliani (1997) proposed M²: combine the fund with the risk-free asset in the proportion that gives it the market's volatility, then compare its return with the market's, $M^2 = r_f + S_p\,\sigma_M - \bar R_M$.

## Which measure to use

The measures count different risks. Which one to use depends on the fund's place in the investor's total wealth, that is, on which part of the fund's risk the investor actually bears.

> **Check question C2**
> 
> An investor holds only one stock fund plus the risk-free asset. Fund A: Sharpe ratio 0.45, Treynor ratio 6. Fund B: Sharpe ratio 0.38, Treynor ratio 9. In choosing, he should mainly look at:
> 
> (A) The Sharpe ratio, choosing A
> (B) The Treynor ratio, choosing B
> (C) The two measures disagree, so he cannot decide
> (D) The average return, choosing the higher one
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

If the fund is only a small part of a well-diversified portfolio, most of its firm-specific risk is diversified away in the whole portfolio, and what matters is its beta and alpha: look at the Treynor ratio or Jensen's alpha. If an active fund is added to a passive index portfolio, its alpha must be weighed against the firm-specific risk it adds: look at the information ratio. Treynor and Black (1973) showed that when the active fund is added in the best proportion, the portfolio's Sharpe ratio satisfies $S^2 = S_M^2 + IR^2$ (Exercises Question 1).

The choice of benchmark matters just as much. Lesson 4.6, "Multifactor Models" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-6-multifactor-models/#fama-french showed that a fund tilted toward small value stocks shows an alpha by the CAPM, which may disappear with a three- or four-factor model (adding momentum). A fund's benchmark should match its investment style; choosing a benchmark that is easy to beat makes performance look better than it is. Also, a manager's timing (changing beta) and style drift during the period distort measures computed with a fixed beta.

## Luck or skill

Even with the right measure, there is a harder question: is the performance luck or skill? The estimation error of alpha is large (Lesson 4.5, "The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-5-single-index-model/#estimation). If a fund's true information ratio is $IR$ and alpha is estimated from $T$ years of annual data, its t-value (t-statistic) is about

$$
t \approx IR \times \sqrt{T}
$$

**Figure 2-1** Years of track record and the t-value of alpha. The solid line is the expected t-value $IR\sqrt{T}$, the shaded band is the 95% range of the t-value, and the dashed lines are the 95% range for a manager with no skill (±1.96).
- This figure has no drawing instructions yet: give the learner the link to the web page and say what to change and what to observe.
- What the learner should observe: First, with an information ratio of 0.3, see how many years the expected t-value needs to rise above the upper dashed line, and how much the band overlaps the area between the dashed lines at 20 years; then raise the information ratio and see how the number of years changes.
- Interactive figure on the web page (the learner can also open it): https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-9-performance-evaluation/#fig-2-1

>

> 
> (A) Falls to about a quarter
> (B) Falls by half

> (D) Rises, because greater skill is harder to prove
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

An information ratio of 0.5 is already considered very good active management, yet even then the expected t-value takes about 15 years to reach 1.96. And there are thousands of funds, some of which will have outstanding long records by chance even with no skill at all (multiple testing).

> **Check question C4**
> 
> If fund performance comes mainly from skill rather than luck, funds that did well in the past should tend to do better than other funds in the future too.
> 
> (True or false)
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

The research findings: Carhart (1997) found that the funds with the best performance in one year are only slightly above average the next year, and the edge mostly disappears after fees and trading costs; the worst funds tend to stay bad, mainly because of high fees and high turnover. Fama and French (2010) used simulation to compare the distribution of alphas of US active stock funds with the distribution if none had skill, and found that after fees few funds have enough skill to cover their costs.

## Survivorship bias

Funds that do badly are often closed or merged into other funds, disappearing from databases and from fund companies' advertising. Historical performance computed only from surviving funds overstates how active management actually did; this is called **survivorship bias**. A similar problem is backfill bias: hedge funds join a database only after building a good record, and bring their earlier performance with them.

Fund companies also make use of this: a company that runs many funds advertises only its best ones and quietly merges away those that do badly. When looking at a fund's record, ask how many funds it was picked from.

> **Check question C5**
>

>

> (B) Too low
> (C) Unbiased, because few funds are closed
> (D) Unbiased, because closed funds are just small
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

## Summary

- The Sharpe ratio counts total risk, the Treynor ratio and Jensen's alpha count systematic risk, and the information ratio relates alpha to firm-specific risk; M² turns the Sharpe ratio into a rate of return.
- For a small part of a diversified portfolio use alpha or the Treynor ratio; for a fund added to an index portfolio use the information ratio, $S^2 = S_M^2 + IR^2$; the choice depends on which part of the risk the investor actually bears.
- The benchmark should match the style; factor exposures can be mistaken for alpha.
- The t-value of alpha is about $IR\sqrt{T}$, so telling luck from skill needs a long record; performance persists only weakly.
- Survivorship bias and selective advertising overstate the performance of active management.

Assign them after the lesson. Answers and grading points are in the key file.

**Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)**

The market's expected return is 9% with a standard deviation of 16%, and the risk-free rate is 3%. Active fund P has an expected return of 12%, a standard deviation of 24% and a beta of 1.1.
(a) What are P's Sharpe ratio and Jensen's alpha? Compare with the market's Sharpe ratio.
(b) A colleague says: "P's Sharpe ratio is no higher than the market's, so buying some P in addition to an index fund will not improve the portfolio." Use P's information ratio and the Treynor–Black result $S^2 = S_M^2 + IR^2$ to evaluate this statement. How does the conclusion differ for an investor who holds only P?

**Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)**

A news story says: "This fund manager has beaten her benchmark 10 years in a row. If it were luck, the chance of beating it in any year would be one half, and the chance of 10 years in a row less than one in a thousand, so she must have skill." There are 2,000 funds of this kind.
(a) Suppose no manager has skill, each beats the benchmark with a 50% chance each year, independently across years and funds. How many of the 2,000 funds would you expect to beat the benchmark 10 years in a row? What is the probability that at least one does?
(b) Over the 10 years she beat the benchmark by 2 percentage points a year on average, with a tracking error of 4 percentage points. What is the t-value of her excess return? Using (a), evaluate the story.

**Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)**

A research firm says: "Over the past 15 years, US active stock funds returned 7.5% a year on average, against 6.5% for index funds, so active management beat the index by 1 percentage point a year on average." Its data include only surviving funds. In fact there were 100 such funds 15 years ago, of which 40 were closed or merged during the period, having returned 3% a year on average while they existed. For simplicity, average across funds with equal weights, giving every fund the same weight.
(a) Including all funds, what is the average annual return of active funds? By how many percentage points does survivorship bias overstate the average?
(b) Evaluate the research firm's statement. If an investor had picked an active fund at random 15 years ago, how would his expected result differ from what the firm says?

**Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)**

A fund has a beta of 0.7. Its marketing says: "Last year the market fell 30% but we fell only 20%, proof of the manager's skill at controlling risk." For simplicity, assume a risk-free rate of 0.
(a) By the CAPM, how much should the fund have fallen last year? What is its Jensen's alpha?
(b) The year before, the market rose 35% and the fund rose 25%. What was that year's alpha? Evaluate the marketing claim. When would "falling less in down markets" show skill?
